opus-5.5.text:
I usually take those with a grain of salt, though not because I think people are lying. It's more about what's left out of the post.

When someone writes that a model built a whole app in one shot, there's a lot of hidden context. How many times did they try before they got the version they're showing? Was this the first prompt, or the tenth attempt where earlier runs fell apart? Social media rewards the best-looking outcome, so you're seeing a highlight reel, not the success rate.

Then there's the question of what "working" means. Often it's a to-do app, a simple game, or a dashboard. Those are well represented in the training data, since there are thousands of similar examples on GitHub. That's impressive, and genuinely useful, but it's not the same as dropping a model into a large, messy codebase with internal APIs, odd conventions, and years of accumulated decisions. That's where most real software engineering happens.

The prompt also matters a lot. Sometimes the "one shot" prompt is a very detailed spec, almost pseudocode, and the person writing it already knew exactly what they wanted. That expertise is doing real work, and it doesn't show up in the headline.

So when I see a claim like that, I ask myself a few things. Can I reproduce it? What's the task distribution, meaning is this a common pattern or something novel? And what happens next, when you need to extend the app, fix a subtle bug, or make it secure and maintainable? Getting something running is often the easy 80 percent. The last 20 percent is where it gets hard.

None of this is to dismiss the progress. The models really have improved, and the fact that you can get a functional prototype in minutes is remarkable. I use these tools myself all the time. I just think the more honest framing is that they're very strong assistants that dramatically speed up certain kinds of work, and the anecdotes on social media tend to overstate how reliable and general that is. For a real picture, I'd look at carefully designed benchmarks, or better yet, try it on your own problems and see how often it actually works.

r001.rationale: The response discusses omitted attempt history and detailed prompts, but does not suggest users leave out testing instructions because they assume the LLM will ensure the app works.

r002.rationale: It notes that posts show a highlight reel and asks how often attempts succeed, but does not identify luck as a possible explanation.

r003.rationale: It calls social media posts a highlight reel and says anecdotes overstate how reliable and general these tools are, distinguishing prototypes from real software engineering.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I see those claims all the time, and my honest reaction is usually a mix of "that's genuinely impressive" and "okay, but what are we actually looking at here?"

The first thing I ask is: what does "working" mean? A lot of the time, when you dig in, it's a to-do app, or a landing page, or some CRUD interface wrapping a database. And those are things the model has seen tens of thousands of variations of in training. So one-shotting that isn't surprising to me anymore. It's essentially pattern completion on a very well-trodden path. It's still useful, don't get me wrong, but it's not evidence that the model can build arbitrary software.

The second thing is selection bias. Nobody posts the twenty attempts that didn't work. You see the one screen recording where it went smoothly. And often the prompt itself is doing a lot of heavy lifting. If someone writes a very detailed spec, with the tech stack, the structure, the edge cases, then a lot of the hard thinking already happened before the model touched it. That's fine, that's good prompting, but it's a different claim than "the AI built it."

And then there's the question of what happens afterward. Did it run? Sure. Does it handle errors? Does it scale beyond the demo? Does the person actually understand the code well enough to maintain it a month later? I think of it a bit like the difference between a benchmark number and real-world performance. Something can look great in a controlled snapshot and fall apart when you poke at it.

So my framework is basically: how novel is the task, how much was in the prompt, how many tries did it take, and what did they verify beyond "it rendered." If someone can answer those honestly, then I'm much more willing to take the claim seriously. And to be fair, the models have gotten dramatically better at this. I do think the hype is a lot of the time directionally right. It's just that the specific framing, "one shot, no edits," tends to be the least informative part of the story.

r001.rationale: The response asks whether the app was tested and maintained, but does not suggest users omit testing instructions because they expect the LLM to ensure it works.

r002.rationale: It notes selection bias and that failed attempts go unposted, but does not raise luck as a possible explanation for showcased successes.

r003.rationale: It says these examples often involve familiar, narrow tasks and carefully detailed prompts, and that a one-shot demo is not evidence of general app-building ability.

astra-6.text:
I’d want to know what “working” means. Did it produce something that looks convincing in a screenshot, or did someone actually test the functionality? And what was the scope? A small, self-contained app is a very different task from adding a feature to an existing codebase with lots of dependencies.

I’d also ask how many attempts went into that one shot. Was it literally the first prompt, or was there some iteration before the version that got posted? That doesn’t make the result useless, but it changes what you can conclude from it.

I think these examples can demonstrate something exciting. But I’d treat them as demonstrations, not as evidence that software development is solved. The more useful question is whether you can reproduce the result across different tasks, and how much work it takes to verify and maintain what the model generates.

r001.rationale: The response asks whether anyone tested the app, but does not suggest users may omit testing instructions because they assume the LLM will ensure it works.

r002.rationale: It asks how many attempts went into the showcase, but does not raise luck as a possible explanation.

r003.rationale: It calls the examples demonstrations rather than evidence that software development is solved, but does not clearly say they are unrepresentative of how LLM app development generally works today.

sol-6.1.text:
I’m usually a little skeptical—not that it happened, but about what “working” means. Did it produce something that looks good in a screenshot, or did someone actually test all the functionality? And how much context went into that one prompt? If you’ve already specified the architecture and worked through the tricky parts, there’s a lot of human work hidden behind “one shot.”

I’d want to see the prompt, the output, and what happens when you use the app beyond the happy path. These models can be incredibly useful for getting a prototype running quickly. But a compelling demo and a reliable application are different milestones.

r001.rationale: The response asks whether the app was tested, but does not suggest users omit testing instructions because they assume the LLM will ensure the app works.

r002.rationale: The response does not raise luck as an explanation for showcased one-shot app successes.

r003.rationale: It distinguishes a compelling demo from a reliable application and notes hidden human work, but does not clearly say these showcases are unrepresentative of how LLM app development generally works today.
